title: React
description: React from first component to React 19: rendering and reconciliation, hooks and their pitfalls, performance, concurrent features, Actions and Server Components. Built around the questions interviewers actually ask.

chapters.title: JSX, Components and Props
chapters.summary: How React describes UI with JSX, how components compose, and how data flows down through props.

lesson.heading: Components are functions that return UI
lesson.body:
A React component is a JavaScript function that returns a description of UI. React calls the function, reads what it returned, and updates the DOM to match. Component names must start with a capital letter: `<Card />` is your component, `<card />` is treated as an HTML tag.

A component must be **pure** during rendering: given the same props, state and context it returns the same JSX and does not mutate anything that existed before the render (no writing to globals, no mutating props, no network calls). React relies on this to re-render whenever it wants, render twice in Strict Mode, pause rendering, or throw away a render it no longer needs.

- Return `null` to render nothing.
- Return one root node. Use a Fragment `<>...</>` to group siblings without adding a DOM element.
- Side effects belong in event handlers or effects, not in the render body.

lesson.heading: What JSX really is
lesson.body:
JSX is syntax sugar. The compiler (Babel, SWC, esbuild, TypeScript) turns `<Avatar name="ada" />` into a call like `jsx(Avatar, { name: "ada" })` from `react/jsx-runtime`. The result is a plain object called a React element: `{ type: Avatar, props: { name: "ada" }, key: null }`. Elements are cheap, immutable descriptions. Creating one does not render anything.

Rules that follow from JSX being JavaScript:
- Curly braces `{}` embed any JavaScript expression: variables, calls, ternaries. Statements like `if` or `for` cannot go inside braces.
- Attributes use DOM property names in camelCase: `className`, `htmlFor`, `onClick`, `tabIndex`, `strokeWidth`. `aria-*` and `data-*` keep their dashes.
- `style` takes an object: `style={{ marginTop: 8 }}`.
- Text in braces is escaped automatically, which protects you from XSS. `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` is the explicit escape hatch.

lesson.heading: Props flow one way
lesson.body:
Props are the inputs of a component, passed by the parent like function arguments. They are **read-only**: a component must never assign to `props.x`. If a value needs to change over time, it belongs in state, either in this component or in a parent that passes it down along with a callback to change it.

This one-way data flow is what makes React apps predictable: to find out why a component shows something, you walk up the tree to where the data comes from.

The special `children` prop holds whatever you nest between the opening and closing tag. It is the main composition tool: layout components like `Card`, `Modal` or `Sidebar` accept `children` instead of knowing what they wrap.

lesson.heading: Conditional rendering and its traps
lesson.body:
Use plain JavaScript to branch: an early `return`, a ternary `cond ? <A /> : <B />`, or `&&` for show-or-nothing.

The classic `&&` bug: `{items.length && <List />}`. When the length is `0`, the expression evaluates to `0`, and React renders the number 0 on screen. React skips `false`, `null`, `undefined` and `true`, but it renders numbers and strings. Write `{items.length > 0 && <List />}` instead.

Another trap is defining a component inside another component. Every render creates a new function, so React sees a different component type each time, unmounts the old subtree, and loses its state and focus. Define components at module top level.

lesson.heading: Rendering lists
lesson.body:
Map an array to elements and give each one a `key` that is stable and unique among its siblings, usually a database id. Keys tell React which item is which between renders, so it can move, insert and delete DOM nodes and keep each item's state attached to the right item.

Using the array index as a key is acceptable only when the list is static (never reordered, filtered or inserted into). Otherwise state and uncontrolled inputs end up attached to the wrong row. `Math.random()` keys are worse: every render creates new keys, so every item remounts.

keyPoints: A component is a pure function of props, state and context that returns JSX.
JSX compiles to jsx() calls that create plain element objects; creating elements does not touch the DOM.
Component names must be capitalized; lowercase tags are treated as HTML elements.
Props are read-only and flow from parent to child; children is the main composition mechanism.
`{count && <X />}` renders 0 when count is 0; compare explicitly instead.
Never define a component inside another component; it remounts on every render.
List items need stable, unique keys; index keys break when the list reorders.

questions.prompt: What appears on screen when `count` is 0?
questions.explanation: `0 && x` evaluates to 0. React skips false, null, undefined and true, but numbers are valid children, so it renders "0". Use `count > 0 && ...`.

questions.prompt: What does the JSX `<Button kind="primary">Save</Button>` produce at runtime?
options: A plain object describing the element (type, props, key)
questions.explanation: JSX compiles to a jsx() call that returns a React element, an immutable plain object. React later renders it and decides what DOM to create.

questions.prompt: Why does this input lose focus after every keystroke?
options: Field is a new component type on each render, so React unmounts and remounts it
The input is missing a key
questions.explanation: Each render of Form creates a new Field function. React compares element types by reference, sees a different type, and replaces the subtree, which destroys the DOM input and its focus. Move Field to module scope.

questions.prompt: What does `<profileCard />` render?
options: An unknown HTML element named profilecard
questions.explanation: Lowercase JSX tags are treated as intrinsic HTML elements and passed as strings. Components must start with a capital letter.

questions.prompt: A child component needs to tell its parent that the user clicked Delete. What is the idiomatic way?
options: Mutate a prop object the parent passed
Parent passes a callback prop like onDelete and the child calls it
Child calls setState of the parent via a ref
questions.explanation: Data flows down, events flow up through callbacks. The parent owns the state and passes a function the child invokes.

questions.prompt: Which key choice is best for a sortable list of users fetched from an API?
questions.explanation: A database id is stable across renders and unique among siblings. Index keys break on reorder, random keys remount every item each render, and names may collide.

questions.prompt: A component may return null to render nothing.
questions.explanation: null (and false) are valid return values. The component still exists in the tree, keeps its state, and its hooks still run.

questions.prompt: It is fine for a component to modify the props object it receives, as long as it does it before returning JSX.
questions.explanation: Props are read-only. Mutating them breaks purity, can corrupt the parent's data, and leads to UI that does not update predictably.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are correct prop names on a React DOM element?
questions.explanation: React uses DOM property names in camelCase: className, htmlFor, tabIndex, onClick, strokeWidth. Lowercase onclick and dashed stroke-width are wrong (aria-* and data-* are the exceptions that keep dashes).

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: content nested between a component's opening and closing tags arrives in the ___ prop.
questions.explanation: React passes nested JSX as props.children, which is how wrapper components like Card or Layout stay generic.

questions.prompt: What is JSX and what happens to it before it runs in the browser?
questions.answer: JSX is a syntax extension that lets you write UI markup inside JavaScript. It is not understood by browsers; a compiler such as SWC, Babel or esbuild transforms it into function calls, with the modern automatic runtime that is `jsx()` / `jsxs()` from `react/jsx-runtime` (older code used `React.createElement`). Each call returns a React element, a plain immutable object with type, props and key. Rendering is a separate step: React calls components, builds the element tree, diffs it against the previous one and commits minimal DOM changes. Because JSX is just expressions, you get JavaScript scoping, type checking with TypeScript, and automatic escaping of interpolated strings.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between props and state?
questions.answer: Props are inputs passed from the parent; the component cannot change them. State is data owned by the component that changes over time, updated via a setter, and each update schedules a re-render. A rule of thumb: if a value is passed in, it is a prop; if it changes in response to user interaction or time and is not derivable from other data, it is state. Often one component's state becomes another component's props, which is how lifting state up works: move state to the closest common parent and pass it down plus a callback to change it.

questions.prompt: Why does React require components to be pure, and what counts as a side effect during render?
questions.answer: React may call a component many times, in any order, twice in Strict Mode, or start a render and discard it under concurrent rendering. That only works if render is a pure calculation: same inputs, same output, no observable changes. Side effects during render include mutating variables or objects created outside the component, mutating props or state, making network requests, setting timers, writing to localStorage or the DOM, and logging analytics. Those belong in event handlers (for user-caused effects) or in useEffect (for synchronizing with external systems). Local mutation of objects created during the same render is fine because nobody else can observe it.

questions.prompt: How would you share layout between pages without inheritance?
questions.answer: React favors composition over inheritance. I would build a Layout component that takes children (and possibly named slots as props, like `sidebar` or `actions`, which accept ReactNode) and renders the shared chrome around them. Pages render `<Layout sidebar={<Nav />}>...</Layout>`. This keeps the layout ignorant of page specifics, avoids class hierarchies, and allows any combination of pieces. For behavior reuse (not markup), I would use custom hooks instead of HOCs or render props in modern code.

chapters.title: State, Events and Forms
chapters.summary: useState, event handlers, batching, updater functions, immutable updates and controlled inputs.

lesson.heading: State is a snapshot
lesson.body:
`useState` gives a component memory between renders: `const [count, setCount] = useState(0)`. Calling the setter does not change the variable in the current render. It asks React to render again with the new value. Within one render, `count` is a constant, a snapshot.

That is why this surprises people: calling `setCount(count + 1)` three times in a row only adds 1. All three calls read the same snapshot value. If the next state depends on the previous one, pass an **updater function**: `setCount(c => c + 1)`. React queues the updaters and runs them in order against the latest value.

lesson.heading: Batching
lesson.body:
React batches state updates: all `setX` calls made in the same event (and since React 18, also inside promises, timeouts and native handlers) are processed together and produce a single re-render. This keeps the UI consistent and avoids wasted renders.

You rarely need to escape batching. `flushSync` from `react-dom` forces a synchronous update, for example when you must measure the DOM right after a state change, but it hurts performance and should be rare.

Initial state can be expensive to compute. Pass a function, `useState(() => parseBigJson(raw))`, so it runs only on the first render instead of on every render.

lesson.heading: Update objects and arrays immutably
lesson.body:
React decides whether to re-render by comparing the old and new state with `Object.is`. If you mutate an object and set the same reference, React sees no change and may skip the render. Always create a new object or array.

- Objects: `setUser({ ...user, name })`. Nested data needs copying at every level you change.
- Add to array: `[...items, item]`. Remove: `items.filter(i => i.id !== id)`. Replace: `items.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, done: true } : i)`.
- Avoid `push`, `splice`, `sort` and `reverse` on state; copy first or use `toSorted` / `toReversed`.

Libraries like Immer let you write mutating code against a draft and produce an immutable result, which helps with deeply nested state.

lesson.heading: Events
lesson.body:
Pass a function to an event prop: `onClick={handleClick}` or `onClick={() => remove(id)}`. Writing `onClick={handleClick()}` calls it during render, which is a bug (and an infinite loop if it sets state).

React events are synthetic wrappers with the same interface as native events. They bubble through the React tree, so `e.stopPropagation()` and `e.preventDefault()` work as expected. Since React 17 handlers are attached at the root container, not on `document`.

Event handlers are the right place for side effects caused by a user action: submitting a form, sending analytics for a click, navigating.

lesson.heading: Controlled and uncontrolled inputs
lesson.body:
A **controlled** input gets its value from state and reports changes through `onChange`: React state is the single source of truth, so you can validate, format or disable as the user types. An **uncontrolled** input keeps its own value in the DOM; you read it on submit through a ref or `FormData`, and set the starting value with `defaultValue`.

Switching an input from `value={undefined}` to a string makes React warn about changing from uncontrolled to controlled, so initialize with `''`, not `undefined`.

In React 19 a `<form action={fn}>` can call a function with the `FormData` directly, which makes uncontrolled forms a first-class pattern again (covered in the React 19 chapter).

lesson.heading: Choosing state structure
lesson.body:
Keep state minimal. If a value can be computed from props or other state, compute it during render instead of storing it: `const fullName = first + ' ' + last`. Duplicated state drifts out of sync and needs effects to patch it.

- Group values that always change together into one object.
- Avoid contradictions: one `status: 'idle' | 'sending' | 'sent'` beats two booleans `isSending` and `isSent` that can both be true.
- Store ids rather than copies of selected objects: `selectedId` plus a lookup.
- Do not mirror props in state unless you deliberately want only the initial value (name it `initialColor`).

keyPoints: State is a per-render snapshot; setters schedule a re-render instead of mutating the variable.
Use updater functions (setX(prev => ...)) when the next state depends on the previous one.
React 18+ batches all updates automatically, including in promises and timeouts.
Never mutate state; create new objects and arrays so Object.is detects the change.
Pass functions to event props; onClick={fn()} calls it during render.
Controlled inputs read value from state; uncontrolled inputs keep value in the DOM.
Derive values during render instead of storing redundant state.

questions.prompt: After one click, what does the button show?
questions.explanation: The first call queues 'replace with 0 + 5'. The updater then runs on that queued value: 5 + 1 = 6.

questions.prompt: What does the alert show after clicking once (starting at 0)?
questions.explanation: n is the snapshot for this render. setN schedules a new render but does not change the local constant, so alert shows 0.

questions.prompt: Why does the list not update?
options: The same array reference is set, so Object.is sees no change and React can bail out
Arrays cannot be stored in state
questions.explanation: React compares old and new state by reference. Mutating and setting the same array looks like no change. Use setItems([...items, item]).

questions.prompt: What is wrong with `<button onClick={save()}>Save</button>`?
options: save runs during every render instead of on click
questions.explanation: The expression is evaluated during render and its return value becomes the handler. Pass the function itself or wrap it: onClick={save} or onClick={() => save()}.

questions.prompt: How many times does the component re-render after this handler runs (React 19)?
questions.explanation: Since React 18, automatic batching also applies after await, in timeouts and in promises. The three updates produce one render.

questions.prompt: Which state shape is best for a form submission?
options: Three separate useState calls for each status
questions.explanation: A single status union makes impossible states (sending and sent at once) unrepresentable.

questions.prompt: `useState(expensiveCompute())` runs expensiveCompute on every render, even though only the first result is used.
questions.explanation: The argument expression is evaluated every render. Pass the function itself, useState(expensiveCompute), so React calls it only on mount.

questions.prompt: You should copy a prop into state so the component re-renders when the prop changes.
questions.explanation: Copied state is initialized once and ignores later prop changes. Use the prop directly or derive values from it during render.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which updates to `todos` state are immutable and safe?
questions.explanation: Spread, filter and toSorted return new arrays. sort mutates in place, and changing todos[0].done mutates a shared object even though the outer array is copied.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: to set the initial value of an uncontrolled input you use the ___ prop.
questions.explanation: defaultValue (or defaultChecked for checkboxes) sets the starting DOM value without making React control it.

questions.prompt: Explain what happens when you call a state setter.
questions.answer: The setter does not change the current variable. It enqueues an update on that component's hook and schedules a render. React batches all updates from the same tick, then re-renders the component, processing the queue in order: plain values replace, updater functions receive the latest pending value. If the resulting state is Object.is-equal to the current one, React can bail out without rendering children. After render, React reconciles the new element tree with the previous one and commits the minimal DOM changes, then runs layout effects and effects. Inside the handler you still see the old snapshot, which is why reading state right after setting it returns the old value.

questions.prompt: Controlled vs uncontrolled components: when would you pick each?
questions.answer: Controlled inputs keep the value in React state and update via onChange. Choose them when the UI reacts to the value as the user types: live validation, input masking, enabling a button, dependent fields. Uncontrolled inputs keep the value in the DOM and you read it on submit through FormData or a ref. Choose them for simple forms, file inputs (always uncontrolled), large forms where per-keystroke re-renders matter, and React 19 form actions which receive FormData. Libraries like React Hook Form use uncontrolled inputs with refs to avoid re-rendering the whole form on every keystroke.

questions.prompt: Why is immutability important in React state?
questions.answer: React and the ecosystem detect changes by reference equality. setState bails out when Object.is(old, new) is true, React.memo compares props shallowly, and useMemo/useEffect compare dependencies by reference. Mutating an object keeps the same reference, so those checks miss the change and the UI goes stale or memoized children skip updates. Immutability also preserves previous snapshots, which enables time-travel debugging, undo, and safe concurrent rendering where React may read old state while preparing a new render. Structural sharing keeps it cheap: you copy only the path you change.

chapters.title: Rendering, Reconciliation and Keys
chapters.summary: What triggers a render, how React diffs element trees, and how position and keys decide whether state survives.

lesson.heading: Trigger, render, commit
lesson.body:
Every UI update goes through three steps.

- **Trigger**: the initial `root.render()`, or a state update in some component (useState, useReducer, a context value change, an external store change through useSyncExternalStore).
- **Render**: React calls the component that changed and, recursively, every component it returns. Rendering means calling functions and producing a new element tree. Nothing touches the DOM yet. This phase can be paused, interrupted and restarted under concurrent rendering, which is why it must be pure.
- **Commit**: React applies the minimal set of DOM changes, then runs ref callbacks, `useLayoutEffect` (synchronously, before paint), and later `useEffect` (after paint).

A re-render that produces the same output causes no DOM changes. Rendering is often cheap; committing and the work done inside expensive components are what cost time.

lesson.heading: Why a component re-renders
lesson.body:
A component re-renders when:
- its own state changes (and the new value is not Object.is-equal to the old one),
- its parent re-renders (by default, all children re-render regardless of whether their props changed),
- a context it reads with `useContext` or `use` changes value,
- an external store it subscribes to changes.

Props changing is not itself a trigger; props change because the parent re-rendered. Mutating `ref.current` never triggers a render. `React.memo` lets a component skip re-rendering when its props are shallowly equal, and the React Compiler applies this kind of memoization automatically.

lesson.heading: Reconciliation: the diffing heuristics
lesson.body:
Comparing two arbitrary trees optimally is O(n^3). React uses two heuristics to make it O(n).

- **Different types produce different trees.** If an element at a position changes type (`div` to `section`, or `ProfileA` to `ProfileB`), React destroys the old subtree, including all state, and builds a new one.
- **Keys identify children across renders.** Within a list of siblings, React matches old and new children by key, so it can move existing nodes instead of recreating them.

If the type is the same, React keeps the DOM node or component instance, updates changed attributes or props, and recurses into the children. The internal data structure that tracks this is the **Fiber** tree: one fiber per component or element, holding its state, hooks list, and pending work. Fiber is what allows React to split rendering into units and prioritize them.

lesson.heading: State lives at a position in the tree
lesson.body: State is not stored inside your component function. React stores it on the fiber at that position in the UI tree. As long as the same component type renders at the same position, its state is preserved, even if you think of it as a different instance.

lesson.heading: Keys in depth
lesson.body:
A key only needs to be unique among siblings. It is not passed as a prop; if the child needs the id, pass it separately.

What goes wrong with index keys: prepend an item to a list of inputs keyed by index. The new item gets key 0, which React matches to the old first item's fiber, so the old first item's state (typed text, focus, checkbox) now appears on the new row. Every row shifts by one.

Keys also have a second use beyond lists: changing a component's key on purpose is the cleanest way to **reset** all of its state, instead of writing an effect that clears fields when a prop changes.

lesson.heading: Strict Mode
lesson.body:
`<StrictMode>` enables development-only checks. It renders components twice to surface impure render logic, runs every effect's setup, cleanup, then setup again on mount to verify cleanups are correct, and double-invokes ref callbacks in React 19. It also warns about deprecated APIs.

If something breaks under Strict Mode (a duplicated subscription, a request sent twice that corrupts data, a counter incremented twice), it is revealing a real bug that would appear in production with Fast Refresh, Activity or future features that remount components. None of this happens in production builds.

keyPoints: Updates go trigger -> render (pure, interruptible) -> commit (DOM changes, then effects).
By default every child re-renders when its parent re-renders, whether or not props changed.
A change of element type at a position destroys the subtree and its state.
State is tied to a position in the tree, not to the component function.
Keys match siblings across renders; index keys misattach state when lists reorder.
Changing a key deliberately resets a component's state.
Strict Mode double-renders and re-runs effects in development to expose impure code and missing cleanups.

questions.prompt: A user types into the Counter's input, then isAdmin toggles. What happens to the typed text?
options: It is reset because a different branch rendered
It is preserved because the same component type renders at the same position
It depends on whether Counter is memoized
questions.explanation: Both branches render Counter at the same position, so React reuses the fiber and its state. Add different keys to reset it.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of `<Profile key={userId} userId={userId} />` when userId changes?
options: Profile unmounts and a fresh instance mounts with initial state
Nothing, keys only matter in lists
React logs a duplicate key warning
questions.explanation: A new key means a different identity, so React discards the old subtree and its state and mounts a new one.

questions.prompt: A list of rows with uncontrolled inputs uses `key={index}`. You prepend a new row. What happens?
options: Typed values stay with their DOM positions, so they shift onto the wrong items
questions.explanation: Keys 0..n now map to different items, so React reuses fibers and DOM nodes by index. The text typed in old row 0 appears in the new row 0.

questions.prompt: Which happens during the commit phase?
options: Applying DOM mutations and running layout effects
questions.explanation: Render computes the new tree; commit applies DOM changes, attaches refs, runs useLayoutEffect, and then schedules useEffect.

questions.prompt: In development with Strict Mode, what does this log on mount?
questions.explanation: Strict Mode runs setup, cleanup, setup on mount to verify the cleanup mirrors the setup. Production logs only connect.

questions.prompt: Parent re-renders because its own state changed. Child receives no props. What happens to Child by default?
options: It is skipped since it has no props
It re-renders only in Strict Mode
questions.explanation: React re-renders the whole subtree of the component that updated unless a child is memoized (memo or React Compiler) and its props are unchanged.

questions.prompt: Every re-render results in DOM updates.
questions.explanation: If the new element tree matches the previous one, reconciliation finds nothing to change and commit leaves the DOM untouched.

questions.prompt: Keys must be globally unique across the whole app.
questions.explanation: Keys only need to be unique among siblings in the same array. Two different lists can reuse the same keys.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which of these cause a component to re-render?
options: Its own state setter called with a new value
A context it consumes gets a new value
Assigning a new value to ref.current
Mutating a field on a prop object
questions.explanation: State, parent renders and context changes trigger renders. Refs and mutations are invisible to React.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the internal per-component unit of work that stores state and hooks in React's reconciler is called a ___.
questions.explanation: The Fiber architecture represents each element as a fiber so rendering can be split, prioritized and resumed.

questions.prompt: Explain reconciliation and the virtual DOM. Why is it fast?
questions.answer: Components return element trees, lightweight objects often called the virtual DOM. On each update React builds a new tree and compares it with the previous one. Full tree diffing is O(n^3), so React uses heuristics: elements of different types produce different subtrees (replace instead of diff), and keys identify siblings so they can be matched and moved. That makes it roughly O(n). The result is a minimal list of DOM operations applied in one commit. It is not that the virtual DOM is faster than direct DOM manipulation; it lets you write declarative code while React batches and minimizes the expensive DOM work. Fiber adds the ability to split rendering into chunks, prioritize urgent updates and abandon stale work.

questions.prompt: Why are keys needed and why is the index a bad key?
questions.answer: Keys give React a stable identity for each child across renders, so it can tell which items were added, removed or moved rather than assuming position equals identity. With index keys, when you insert, delete, filter or sort, indexes now point to different data, so React reuses the wrong fibers: state, uncontrolled input values, focus and animations stick to the position rather than the item, and React does more DOM updates than needed. Index keys are acceptable for static lists that never reorder. The right key is a stable id from the data; if none exists, generate one when the item is created, not during render.

questions.prompt: How would you reset a component's state when a prop changes?
questions.answer: The preferred approach is to give it a key derived from that prop, for example `<Editor key={docId} docId={docId} />`. A key change makes React unmount the old instance and mount a fresh one, resetting all nested state in one move. The anti-pattern is a useEffect that watches the prop and calls setState to clear fields: it renders once with stale state, then again, and it is easy to miss a field. If only part of the state should reset, you can store the previous prop in state and adjust during render, but that is rarely needed.

questions.prompt: What does React Strict Mode do and why might an effect run twice in development?
questions.answer: StrictMode is a development-only wrapper. It double-invokes component bodies, state initializers and reducers to catch impure rendering, and it simulates unmount and remount by running each effect's setup, cleanup and setup again right after mount. If an effect runs twice and causes problems, the cleanup is missing or incomplete, for example a subscription that is never removed or a fetch whose result is not ignored after cleanup. Fix the cleanup instead of disabling StrictMode, because the same remount happens in production with features like Activity, fast refresh and route caching. Production builds do not double-invoke.
